title: Restriction Enzymes & Sticky vs. Blunt Ends

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: Restriction enzymes are bacterial enzymes that cut double-stranded DNA at specific, sequence-defined recognition sites, and the way each enzyme cuts determines whether the resulting DNA fragment ends are 'sticky' (with short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with a complementary overhang) or 'blunt' (fully double-stranded, with no overhang).
explanation: Restriction enzymes naturally evolved as part of bacterial restriction-modification systems that degrade invading foreign DNA (such as bacteriophage DNA) while the bacterium's own DNA is protected by methylation at the same recognition sites. In molecular cloning, this sequence-specific cutting is exploited to open both a vector and an insert at defined, predictable positions. Sticky-end cuts leave complementary single-stranded overhangs on the two resulting fragments, which can anneal to each other before ligation, generally making a subsequent ligation reaction more efficient and directional than working with blunt ends, which have no overhang to guide reannealing and rely on ligase joining the ends directly.

comparison.example: Short single-stranded overhang left after the cut; complementary sticky ends can base-pair before ligation, often improving ligation efficiency
No overhang; the cut leaves two fully double-stranded ends, which ligate less efficiently and without directional bias from overhang complementarity

commonMisconceptions: Assuming any two restriction enzymes' sticky ends are compatible with each other — only enzymes producing the same overhang sequence (not necessarily the same recognition site) will anneal together.

Forgetting that a vector cut with the same single enzyme at two sites can re-ligate to itself (recircularize) without an insert, which is why some cloning strategies use two different enzymes or include a dephosphorylation step.
